newsitem.title: USA: Clinton undecided on Latin America arms sales.
newsitem.headline: Clinton undecided on Latin America arms sales.

text.p: President Bill Clinton has not made any decision on changing a longstanding U.S. policy of virtually banning high-tech arms sales to Latin America, the White House said on Thursday.

U.S. officials said on Wednesday the outgoing secretaries of state and defence, Warren Christopher and William Perry, had urged Clinton in a memo to end the policy, which could open new markets for the U.S. arms industry.

"The arrival of democracy in all but one of the countries in that region changes the environment in which some of our existing polices might apply," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters on Thursday.

"We have significant security needs in the region too and the fact that these countries are moving toward democracy is encouraging and opens up some commercial opportunities in the arguments made by some who are dealing with this issue," he said. "But I stress that there hasn't been a formal decision on this."

Disclosure of the memo, which follows reports of differences of opinion on the issue among officials in the state and defence departments, prompted a sharp response from State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.

Burns did not deny the memo existed but indicated Christopher had concerns over the risk of an arms race and did not back a big policy change. "If other people are talking (about this issue) at the Pentagon they shouldn't characterise the views of the secretary of state. We don't characterise the views of the secretary of defence from our podium," he said.

Burns said Christopher's views on the issue -- expressed publicly before Congress several months ago -- had not changed. "Absolutely, positively. Whatever the secretary has said on this issue stands," he said.

In his testimony Christopher backed the existing U.S. policy, which essentially called for restraint in approving high-tech arms sales to Latin America but allowed a "case by case" review of requested weapons sales.
One official who declined to be identified told Reuters on Thursday that if a change is decided, "we're talking about a change at the margin rather than any kind of major policy adjustment."
He said the only Latin country that might soon seek a major arms buy was Chile, rumoured to be interested in fighter planes. The Pentagon saw potential demand from Brazil and other countries, too.
Clinton was expected to visit Latin America this year, perhaps in March, and a new policy replacing a decades-old ban could be in place by then, the officials said.
